newsitem.title: USA: Russian former captain wins U.S. environmental prize.
newsitem.headline: Russian former captain wins U.S. environmental prize.

text.p: A retired Russian naval captain who was charged with treason for exposing the danger posed by ageing nuclear submarines was among seven winners of an international environmental prize on Monday.

Other winners of this year's $75,000 Goldman environmental prizes included an American mother who fought a toxic waste incinerator and a British man who took the lead in creating the world's first multinational enforcement body to fight illegal wildlife trade in Africa.
The San Francisco-based Goldman Environmental Foundation awards the prizes annually to grassroots environmentalists from six regions of the world.

"The 1997 winners have demonstrated their commitment to protecting the earth and the benefit of future generations without regard to personal risk," foundation president Richard Goldman said in a statement.

The winner for Europe was Alexander Nikitin, a former Russian naval officer who served on nuclear-powered submarines in the 1980s. After he left the Navy, Nikitin publicised the danger posed by ageing submarines based on the Kola Peninsula, where there are 67 operating nuclear submarines and 52 retired ones, the foundation said.
It said the danger of "catastrophic radioactive contamination, especially from eroded and leaking submarines, is great."

Nikitin, now 44, joined the Bellona Foundation, a Norwegian environmental group, and co-authored a report on the Russian northern fleet. Nikitin was arrested in February 1996 and jailed on charges of high treason, the foundation said, adding that Russian authorities accused him of releasing state secrets. It said Nikitin was freed last December but the charges against him still stand.
Another prize went to American Terri Swearingen, 40, a nurse from Chester, West Virginia, who campaigned to halt the building of the nation's largest toxic waste incinerator in East Liverpool, Ohio.
Concerned that the plant, built near a school, would emit carcinogenic heavy metals, Swearingen led marches and acts of civil disobedience, the foundation said.

While the plant was finally built, Swearingen has prevented other such incinerators from being constructed across the United States and continues to try to have the permits of the East Liverpool incinerator revoked, it said.

Also honoured was Nick Carter, 69, a British man working in Zambia who helped organise a 1992 conference in Lusaka that recommended forming an African inter-governmental task force to fight the illegal trade in protected species.
Carter's efforts came to fruition last December when, under the Lusaka agreement, the world's first multinational enforcement body to fight wildlife crime entered into force, the foundation said.
American biology professor Paul Cox, 43, and Samoan High Chief Fuiono Senio, 66, shared a prize for their efforts to stop logging in a lowland rainforest in Western Samoa.

Another winner was Loir Botor Dingit, 59, paramount chief of the Bentian Tribal Council in Indonesia, who the foundation said galvanised national attention to the sustainable conservation practices of Kalimantan's indigenous peoples and convinced government ministers to support the rights of forest dwellers.

The foundation honoured Juan Pablo Orrego, 47, director of the Group to Save the Bio Bio river in Chile, saying he had repeatedly foiled plans to speed up construction of the Ralco Dam by exposing its potential for environmental and cultural damage.
The prizes were due to be awarded at a ceremony in San Francisco later on Monday.
